{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
[[Image:Suspension.svg|right|thumb|Suspension of a [[circle]]. The original space is in blue, and the collapsed end points are in green.]]In [[topology]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''suspension''' of a [[topological space]] ''X'' is intuitively obtained by stretching ''X'' into a [[cylinder (geometry)|cylinder]] and then collapsing both end faces to points. One views ''X'' as "suspended" between these end points. The suspension of ''X'' is denoted by '''''SX'''''<ref>[[Allen Hatcher]], [https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html ''Algebraic topology.''] Cambridge University Presses, Cambridge, 2002. xii+544 pp. {{isbn|0-521-79160-X}} and {{isbn|0-521-79540-0}}</ref> or '''susp(''X'')'''.<ref name=":03">{{Cite Matousek 2007}}</ref>{{Rp|page=76}} 

There is a variant of the suspension for a [[pointed space]], which is called the '''reduced suspension''' and denoted by '''Σ''X'''''. The "usual" suspension ''SX'' is sometimes called the '''unreduced suspension''', '''unbased suspension''', or '''free suspension''' of ''X'', to distinguish it from Σ''X.'' 

== Free suspension ==
The (free) suspension <math>SX</math> of a [[topological space]] <math>X</math> can be defined in several ways.

'''1.''' <math>SX</math> is the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] <math>(X \times [0,1])/(X\times \{0\})\big/ ( X\times \{1\}).</math> In other words, it can be constructed as follows:

* Construct the [[cylinder (geometry)|cylinder]] <math>X \times [0,1]</math>.
* Consider the entire set <math> X\times \{0\}</math> as a single point ("glue" all its points together).
* Consider the entire set <math> X\times \{1\}</math> as a single point ("glue" all its points together).

'''2'''. Another way to write this is:

<math>SX := v_0 \cup_{p_0}(X \times [0,1])\cup_{p_1} v_1\ =\ \varinjlim_{i \in \{0,1\}} \bigl( (X \times [0,1]) \hookleftarrow (X\times \{i\}) \xrightarrow{p_i} v_i\bigr),</math>

Where <math>v_0, v_1</math> are two [[Point (topology)|points]], and for each ''i'' in {0,1},  <math>p_i</math> is the [[Projection (mathematics)|projection]] to the point <math>v_i</math> (a function that maps everything to <math>v_i</math>). That means, the suspension <math>SX</math> is the result of constructing the [[cylinder (geometry)|cylinder]] <math>X \times [0,1]</math>, and then [[adjunction space|attaching]] it by its faces, <math>X\times\{0\}</math> and <math>X\times\{1\}</math>, to the points <math>v_0, v_1</math> along the projections <math>p_i: \bigl( X\times\{i\} \bigr)\to v_i</math>.

'''3.''' One can view <math>SX</math> as two [[cone (topology)|cones]] on ''X,'' [[adjunction space|glued together]] at their base.

'''4.''' <math>SX</math> can also be defined as the [[join (topology)|join]] <math>X\star S^0,</math> where <math>S^0</math> is a [[discrete space]] with two points.<ref name=":03" />{{Rp|page=76}}

'''5'''. In [[Homotopy type theory]], <math>SX</math> is defined as a higher inductive type generated by

S: <math>SX</math>

N:<math>SX</math>

<math>Merid: \bigl( X\bigr)\to (N=S)</math><ref>{{Cite web |title=suspension type in nLab |url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/suspension+type |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=ncatlab.org}}</ref>

=== Properties ===
In rough terms, ''S'' increases the dimension of a space by one: for example, it takes an ''n''-[[sphere]] to an (''n'' +&thinsp;1)-sphere for ''n'' &ge; 0.

Given a [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous map]]  <math>f:X\rightarrow Y,</math> there is a continuous map <math>Sf:SX\rightarrow SY</math> defined by <math>Sf([x,t]):=[f(x),t],</math> where square brackets denote [[equivalence class]]es. This makes <math>S</math> into a [[functor]] from the [[category of topological spaces]] to itself.

==Reduced suspension==
If ''X'' is a [[pointed space]] with basepoint ''x''<sub>0</sub>, there is a variation of the suspension which is sometimes more useful. The '''reduced suspension''' or '''based suspension''' &Sigma;''X'' of ''X'' is the quotient space:

:<math>\Sigma X = (X\times I)/(X\times\{0\}\cup X\times\{1\}\cup \{x_0\}\times I)</math>.

This is the equivalent to taking ''SX'' and collapsing the line (''x''<sub>0</sub> &times; ''I''{{space|hair}}) joining the two ends to a single point. The basepoint of the pointed space &Sigma;''X'' is taken to be the equivalence class of (''x''<sub>0</sub>,&thinsp;0).

One can show that the reduced suspension of ''X'' is homeomorphic to the [[smash product]] of ''X'' with the [[unit circle]] ''S''<sup>1</sup>.

:<math>\Sigma X \cong S^1 \wedge X</math>

For [[well-behaved]] spaces, such as [[CW complex]]es, the reduced suspension of ''X'' is [[homotopy equivalent]] to the unbased suspension.

=== Adjunction of reduced suspension and loop space functors ===
&Sigma; gives rise to a functor from the [[category of pointed spaces]] to itself. An important property of this functor is that it is [[left adjoint]] to the functor <math>\Omega</math> taking a pointed space <math>X</math> to its [[loop space]] <math>\Omega X</math>. In other words, we have a [[natural isomorphism]]

:<math> \operatorname{Maps}_*\left(\Sigma X,Y\right) \cong \operatorname{Maps}_*\left(X,\Omega Y\right)</math>

where <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are pointed spaces and <math>\operatorname{Maps}_*</math> stands for continuous maps that preserve basepoints. This adjunction can be understood geometrically, as follows:  <math>\Sigma X</math> arises out of <math>X</math> if a pointed circle is attached to every non-basepoint of  <math>X</math>, and the basepoints of all these circles are identified and glued to the basepoint of <math>X</math>.  Now, to specify a pointed map from  <math>\Sigma X</math> to <math>Y</math>, we need to give pointed maps from each of these pointed circles to  <math>Y</math>. This is to say we need to associate to each element of <math>X</math> a loop in <math>Y</math> (an element of the loop space  <math>\Omega Y</math>), and the trivial loop should be associated to the basepoint of <math>X</math>: this is a pointed map from <math>X</math> to <math>\Omega Y</math>. (The continuity of all involved maps needs to be checked.)  

The adjunction is thus akin to [[currying]], taking maps on cartesian products to their curried form, and is an example of [[Eckmann–Hilton duality]]. 

This adjunction is a special case of the adjunction explained in the article on [[Smash product|smash products]].

=== Applications ===
The reduced suspension can be used to construct a [[Group homomorphism|homomorphism]] of [[homotopy group]]s, to which the [[Freudenthal suspension theorem]] applies. In [[homotopy theory]], the phenomena which are preserved under suspension, in a suitable sense, make up [[stable homotopy theory]].

== Examples ==
Some examples of suspensions are:''<ref name=":0">{{Cite Matousek 2007}}, Section 4.3</ref>''{{Rp|page=77|location=Exercise.1}}

* The suspension of an [[n-ball]] is homeomorphic to the (n+1)-ball.

==Desuspension==
{{main|Desuspension}}

[[Desuspension]] is an operation partially inverse to suspension.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.forthelukeofmath.com/documents/Wolcott-McTernan-workshop.pdf
|title=Imagining Negative-Dimensional Space|publisher=forthelukeofmath.com|access-date=2015-06-23|first=Luke |last=Wolcott}}</ref>
